newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan plans to privatise phosphate rail link.
newsitem.headline: Jordan plans to privatise phosphate rail link.

text.p: Jordan said on Tuesday it planned to privatise the only railway ferrying phosphates from southern mines to the Red Sea port city of Aqaba to meet growing export demands.
Transport Minister Nasser al-Lawzi said six international consultants had offered to prepare technical work for the privatisation and a French firm was close to concluding a feasibility study.
"Due to the urgency of this project and lack of adequate finance...a decision was taken last week to issue invitations to international consultants," Lawzi told Reuters.
He said the international consultants would "work out a concession agreement and (provide) assistance in the bidding and evaluation process and final negotiation of a concession contract."

The railway, built in the 1970s to carry 1.5 million tonnes of phosphates a year from the southern al-Hasa and al-Abyad mines to Aqaba, will have to handle 10 million tonnes annually by the year 2000 after major expansion and investments in the nearby Shidiya mine which holds Jordan's largest reserves.
Jordan's current output of five million tonnes a year makes it one of the world's largest phosphate producers. The industry is one of the impoverished kingdom's main hard-currency earners.
The state-run Aqaba Railway Corporation is currently operating the 292-km (183 mile) narrow-gauge rail which links Abyad and Hassa to Aqaba.

Around $50 million in private funds is be needed to build a rail connection with nearby Shidiya, refurbish old locomotives and buy new ones, Lawzi added. Part of the transport is currently down in an ageing fleet of 7,000 waggons.
He said a consultant company would have to prepare the terms of reference and bidding documents by the start of next year.
"After that, we will invite consortiums to do the construction work and run the operation."
Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti's government is bent on pushing forward long-delayed steps for privatisation of major state enterprises to inch the country towards a market economy.
Shidiya mine, with its high grade phosphate, is by far the lowest-cost producer of Jordan's three operating mines. It contains one billion of the country's 1.5 billion tonnes in proven reserves.
Production there has been stepped up since 1988. The two lower-grade mines will be gradually phased out in coming years.
